analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 100% extra tax on bonuses over $100,000 paid by bailed-out financial firms.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and died there despite 41 Democratic sponsors and cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the tax code to add a 100% surtax on bonuses over $100,000 paid to employees of companies that received federal rescue money under the Troubled Asset Relief Program. It was a direct response to public anger over large bonuses at firms kept afloat by taxpayer bailouts during the 2008 financial crisis. The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and the general public, who paid for the bank rescues and would recoup bonus payments made with federal bailout money. Rank-and-file employees at bailed-out firms earning under $100,000 in bonuses would pay nothing extra.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a new tax bracket that taxes TARP bonuses at a 100% rate on top of normal income tax, meaning bonus income over $100,000 from a bailed-out firm would be fully recaptured by the federal government.

It applies to anyone receiving a bonus from a TARP-assisted company or from a company that acquired a major portion of a TARP-assisted business, and it treats parent companies and subsidiaries as one entity so bonuses could not be shifted to affiliates to escape the tax.
Bonuses at or under $100,000 per year would be unaffected, so ordinary employees at bailed-out firms would not be touched by the new tax.

analysis.who_pays: Executives and highly paid employees of firms that received TARP bailout funds, whose bonuses above $100,000 would be taxed away entirely. The firms themselves would face pressure to change compensation practices.

drawbacks.text: The tax falls on the bonus recipients, not the firms, so a company could still pay the bonus and simply let the employee absorb the tax, or raise base salaries to offset it, limiting how much money actually returns to taxpayers.

Targeting a defined group of workers with a punitive tax rate raises concerns about using the tax code to punish an unpopular group, and critics warned such measures could make it hard for troubled firms to retain staff needed to wind down their holdings; supporters replied that bonuses at firms surviving on federal money were the real unfairness.
The bill applies only to TARP assistance and would not reach bonuses at bailed-out firms that took other forms of federal support, leaving gaps in coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is narrow but real: taxpayers would claw back roughly the full amount of large bonuses paid by firms that survived on federal rescue money, while the cost falls on a small, highly compensated group and on firms' ability to pay for talent. The design has genuine weaknesses — it taxes individuals rather than firms, which limits the recapture — but the sum at stake, in the context of a public that had just funded the banking system's rescue, was substantial.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 16, 2009 by Rep. Steve Israel with four original cosponsors, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
Forty House Democrats cosponsored the bill in total.
No further action was ever recorded: the bill received no subcommittee or committee vote, no floor vote, and no companion action in the Senate before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives and other highly paid employees of TARP-funded firms kept their large bonuses without the additional tax, and the firms avoided the compensation scrutiny the bill would have brought. The Ways and Means Committee, by never acting, preserved the status quo that the bill's 41 supporters wanted to change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: TARP bonus recipients and the tax committee

for.name: Rep. Steve Israel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means.

for.name: 40 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, signaling committee members had majority-party support but no floor vote was ever scheduled.

for.name: Reps. Braley, Chandler, McCarthy of NY, and Massa
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no recorded action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the party controlled none of the levers needed to move it out of committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republicans signed on, and the bill never advanced far enough to produce a floor vote that would have revealed the full partisan split.

industries.note: Bonus income over $100,000 from bailed-out firms would have been taxed at 100%, effectively recapturing bonuses paid with the help of federal rescue money. Because the bill died, this group kept the bonuses with no additional tax.

The firms would not have paid the tax directly, but it would have pressured them to restructure executive compensation and risked driving out staff needed to unwind troubled assets. Their direct financial exposure was smaller than their employees'.
